headline: Ninau is from classical 担ふ (ninafu), 荷 (ni, “load”) plus なふ (nafu, verb-forming suffix).
Kakumei is from Middle Chinese 革命 (“to switch to a new dynasty/regime”), and Fukuzawa Yukichi used it to translate English revolution.
Giri is from Middle Chinese 義理, which first meant “righteous principle” and narrowed in Japan during the Muromachi and Edo periods.
Hitojichi is 人 (hito, “person”) plus 質 (shichi, “pawn, hock”), and first meant “indentureship”, with “hostage” arising by extension.
Tegaru is from the stem of 手軽い (tegarui), first cited to a text from 1754.
シナリオ is borrowed from English scenario, from Italian scenario, and is first attested in 1928.
ワット is borrowed from English watt.
Fundan was originally 不断 (fudan).
Sedai is ultimately from Middle Chinese 世代 and first appears in the early 1500s.
Mangetsu is from Middle Chinese 滿月, literally “full + moon”.
Teppen is a shift from 天辺 (tehen).
コントロール is from English control.
オートマチック is from English automatic.
Hanayaka is 花 (hana, “flower”) plus やか (-yaka, “seeming like”), and the source compares English flowery.
Ninmei is from Middle Chinese 任命, “burden, charge + command”.
ポイント is from English point.
ドライブイン is English drive-in, equal to ドライブ (doraibu) plus イン (in).
バック is borrowed from English back.
スポーツカー is from English sports car.
Meiryō is from Middle Chinese 明瞭.
ケース is borrowed from English case.
Kakageru is a regular shift from Classical Japanese 掲ぐ (kakagu), itself a contraction of 掻き上ぐ (kakiagu).
フロント is borrowed from English front.
In hanpatsu, 発 is a daiyōji replacing 撥.
Ryōshō is 了 (ryō, “comprehend”) plus 承 (shō, “agree to”), and 了 is a daiyōji replacing 諒.
Otozureru is from the Classical Japanese verb otoduru, analysable as 音 (oto, “sound”) plus 連れる (tsureru, “to bring along; to accompany”), with rendaku.
Masashiku is the adverbial form of the classical adjective 正し (masashi).
プラス is from English plus.
Butsuzō is 仏 (butsu, “Buddha”) plus 像 (zō, “image”).
ドライ is borrowed from English dry.
Nagedasu is 投げる (nageru, “to throw”) plus 出す (dasu, “to send out”).
